hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a low base salary with the expectation of catching up through performance raises
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Salary increases at most companies are percentage-based, so a lower base permanently compounds into lower absolute pay even with identical performance ratings — the gap never closes organically
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New hires who negotiated poorly at offer stage and are counting on internal raises to correct the gap

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a below-market offer expecting performance to close the gap over time
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Recruiter or manager reassures the candidate that good work will be rewarded with raises comparable to peers — candidate takes this at face value and deprioritizes negotiation at offer stage
failure_patterns.consequence: Because raises are applied as a percentage of base, a lower starting salary creates a permanent compounding disadvantage; the candidate never reaches parity with peers who started higher
warning_signs: Recruiter says 'prove yourself first and we'll make it right'
Candidate thinks 'I'll negotiate after I show my value in the role'

industry_realities.common_belief: If you perform well after joining, the company will raise your salary to match peers who started at a higher base
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most companies — especially large or publicly listed ones — apply raises as a fixed percentage tied to a performance band. A lower base means even an identical performance rating yields a lower absolute raise. The starting gap widens over time, not narrows.
industry_realities.implication: The only reliable moment to close a compensation gap is at the offer stage. Candidates should treat the offer negotiation as their primary leverage window, not a preliminary round before the 'real' negotiation inside the job.

industry_realities.common_belief: Re-negotiating after receiving a formal offer is risky because the company will see it as bad faith or opportunistic
industry_realities.actual_reality: This belief is stated in the top answer but presented as a personal opinion with zero upvotes and no corroboration. It may reflect a specific cultural or market context (likely China domestic) rather than a universal rule. In many professional markets, post-offer negotiation is standard and expected.
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not treat this framing as a universal rule. Context — country, industry, seniority level, and whether a competing offer exists — heavily determines how post-offer negotiation is received.

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Accepts the initial offer to appear cooperative, assumes strong performance will lead to salary correction later
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats the offer stage as the primary and most powerful negotiation window; knows that post-hire raises are structurally capped by percentage bands and will not close a base salary gap
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A candidate who defers negotiation loses compounding salary value across the entire tenure at the company

community_misconceptions.misconception: If you work hard and get good performance reviews, the company will eventually raise your pay to be equal to colleagues who started at a higher salary
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Managers and recruiters sometimes imply this during offer conversations to deflect negotiation; it feels meritocratic and fair — if you earn it, you'll get it
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Performance raises are applied as percentages of your current base within predefined bands. The same performance rating on a lower base produces a smaller absolute raise than on a higher base. The structural gap persists and often grows.
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who defer negotiation and rely on performance to correct the gap find themselves permanently underpaid relative to peers, with no internal mechanism to close it

community_misconceptions.misconception: Re-negotiating after receiving an offer signals bad faith and will get the offer rescinded or damage the relationship
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Stated confidently by the top answer; feels intuitive because the offer represents a completed internal process — pushing back feels like disrupting it
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Post-offer negotiation is standard practice in most professional and tech hiring markets. Employers expect it. The actual risk level depends on market context, how negotiation is framed, and whether a competing offer exists — not on the mere act of asking.
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who believe this forgo negotiation entirely at the offer stage, locking in a lower base with no path to correction

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate asks whether they can re-negotiate after receiving an offer, framing it as a risk to the offer itself
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Fear of losing the offer entirely — catastrophizing a normal professional exchange as a high-stakes threat
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate accepts the first offer without pushback, or asks permission-seeking questions that signal they won't actually negotiate
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the question: the offer is not a fragile object that breaks if touched. Ask instead: 'What is my leverage right now, and what is the realistic downside of asking?' This separates perceived risk from actual risk.
